title: ChatGPT mobile app gets voice-based agentic features
description: In Brief Posted: 10:00 AM PDT · September 23, 2026  Image Credits:Samuel Boivin/NurPhoto / Getty Images  		 							 											 									 					 	  OpenAI announced on Wednesday that it is bringing voice-based...
body:
In Brief
Posted:
10:00 AM PDT · September 23, 2026

Image Credits:Samuel Boivin/NurPhoto / Getty Images

		
							
											
									
					
	

OpenAI announced on Wednesday that it is bringing voice-based agentic features to mobile, allowing users to trigger workflows like drafting documents or summarizing emails. 
Plus and Pro users will be able to use the Work tab on their phone to create a document, draft an email, or summarize Slack messages, for instance. These subscribers can do things like build sites, create presentations, use the cloud browser, and also access other areas like finances in ChatGPT. Free and Go users, meanwhile, will get to work with plugins and connected apps.
OpenAI said ChatGPT’s voice conversations will have richer text output. Plus, users will be able to switch between text and voice easily. They can also start working on a conversation on the go and resume it on desktop.
The feature arrives as an increasing number of users are turning to voice to issue commands to AI assistants for complex tasks.
In July, OpenAI launched its new conversational model GPT-Live, and later the company integrated it with the desktop app to let users use their voice to complete tasks in the Work tab or build apps in the Codex tab. The new rollout brings similar capabilities to the mobile app.
Recently, Anthropic made the handoff between mobile and desktop easier and also merged its Cowork and Chat interface. But OpenAI is still keeping chat and workspaces separate.

title: YouTube is making comments more fun — and fandom more lucrative for creators
description: YouTube’s comments section is getting an upgrade, alongside the rollout of other community-focused features such as exclusive paid memberships, the company announced at its Made On YouTube event on Wednesday....
body:
YouTube’s comments section is getting an upgrade, alongside the rollout of other community-focused features such as exclusive paid memberships, the company announced at its Made On YouTube event on Wednesday. Commenters will now be able to respond with GIFs or leave comments from their TVs, while creators will get new tools to support their fan communities, including features to personalize moderation, invite members into VIP-like areas, and give fans new ways to help them make money from their content.
Comments are still one of the main ways YouTube viewers interact with creators’ content, but they’ve often lagged behind other social networks’ commenting features. For instance, TikTok just announced that commenters can respond to videos with their voice and add polls, photo carousels, and Live Photos to their comments. Spotify lets video podcasters use polls and Q&As to engage their audiences.
Image Credits:YouTube
YouTube is finally catching up a bit by adding support for leaving GIFs in comments and letting users comment while watching YouTube on TV. The latter works by voice, not painfully typing out “LOL” on your remote control, YouTube noted.
One of the more interesting additions is a new comment moderation tool that’s personalized to each creator’s needs. Though YouTube already offers a comment moderation filter, creators may want to tailor it more precisely, particularly on live videos, where it’s harder to keep up. For now, the company is calling this personalized moderation an “experiment” and didn’t provide specific technical details about how it works.
Image Credits:YouTube
Other features are meant to help creators grow their fan communities — and make money from that fandom. These arrive at a time when revenue from advertising is no longer the only way creators monetize their videos. 
The company said its Channel Memberships features are evolving, with the addition of paid, members-only communities, where members can share posts and start discussions with other top fans. YouTube will market these communities alongside other memberships on a new “channel memberships” page for viewers, designed to help them discover ones that match their interests.
Hype, a feature that lets fans recommend smaller creators’ videos to others and climb fan leaderboards, will gain new functionality dubbed “Hype with Jewels.” Previously, fans could only “hype” videos three times per week for free. Now they can buy Jewels, a virtual currency of sorts, to hype videos even more, helping to support creators and grow their audience. Fans motivated by clout may also appreciate that their handles will be permanently added to the video’s description.
YouTube said viewers have so far hyped more than 75 million unique videos over 1 billion times.
Image Credits:YouTube
The company’s direct messaging feature for sharing videos with family and friends will also support group chats in the next few months. Users will be able to record quick, raw videos and share them in these conversations, too.
These community-focused features arrived alongside other creator tools, including those for A/B testing, live dubbing, AI-assisted video editing, and more.

title: YouTube will let you build your own algorithm with AI
description: YouTube says it’s going to let you build your own algorithm — well, kind of. The company on Wednesday announced a new feature called custom feeds that allows you to describe, in your own words, the kinds of...
body:
YouTube says it’s going to let you build your own algorithm — well, kind of. The company on Wednesday announced a new feature called custom feeds that allows you to describe, in your own words, the kinds of videos you’d like YouTube to recommend to you.
To create one, you type a description of what you want the feed to be about into a prompt box on YouTube, whether that’s a feed dedicated to a particular interest or one that serves some other purpose. For instance, YouTube suggests you could build a feed of video podcasts to watch during your 30-minute train commute, or you could request videos for a particular mood, like “relaxing commentary videos to unwind with.”
Image Credits:YouTube
The prompt-based feature leverages Google’s Gemini AI model to build the feed around your request, and the resulting feed is then pinned to the top of your YouTube home page in its own tab. Because the feed’s creation is AI-powered, the request can be described in lengthy terms, as you share detailed information about how you want to curate the feed, what it should feature or exclude, what content to prioritize, and more.
The addition follows similar moves by a number of other social networks that have created tools that essentially allow users to build their own algorithms by describing what they want their feed to include and how to present that information to them.
Decentralized social network Bluesky began popularizing this idea years ago as a way to differentiate its service from rivals like X. This year, it rolled out an AI tool, Attie, that makes feed-building even easier. Other services, including Meta’s Threads, Instagram, X, and, more recently, Spotify, have also launched their own feed-building features, many of which are also AI-powered.
Image Credits:YouTube
YouTube believes custom feeds will help users better explore the vast number of videos now hosted on its platform.
“One of the amazing things about being on YouTube is that the world is always at your fingertips,” noted Emily Moxley, VP of Product Management for Viewer AI, in a pre-brief with reporters ahead of the Made On YouTube event on Wednesday, where custom feeds were introduced to the public. “There’s over 20 billion videos in the YouTube corpus, so you’re always one search away from a treasure trove of topics.”
The new feeds, however, will not replace YouTube’s main feed, which features all your recommendations. Instead, you will now be able to easily hop right into whichever feed best suits your purposes when you open the YouTube app.
Support for creating multiple custom feeds will roll out across YouTube on web and mobile, starting next month, the company said.

title: Here’s the trailer for Nathan Fielder’s Elizabeth Holmes documentary, in theaters October 16
description: Image Credits:Justin Sullivan / Getty Images	 	 						7:21 AM PDT · September 23, 2026											  			 We live in a bewildering time, where the world’s most powerful people are trying to make themselves...
body:
Image Credits:Justin Sullivan / Getty Images	
	
						7:21 AM PDT · September 23, 2026											

			
We live in a bewildering time, where the world’s most powerful people are trying to make themselves cyborgs, conquer the inevitability of death, and colonize outer space. But in the midst of such a jarring moment in the history of humanity, the world throws you a bone. In this cursed timeline, we have been gifted something so unfathomable that we could never have imagined it, because even in our wildest dreams, we wouldn’t have come up with something so perfect: a Nathan Fielder documentary about Elizabeth Holmes.
For the uninitiated, Nathan Fielder is a filmmaker and comedian who is known for his uncanny ability to put himself into awkward situations, yet remain in character for so long that it forces everyone involved — even the viewer — to reflect on the essence of their own existence. And then there’s Elizabeth Holmes, the disgraced Theranos startup founder who still denies she did anything wrong, making the world question whether she’s really that naive, or if she’s still playing a game of 5D chess that none of us signed up for.
We are not ready for these two to collide, but get your black turtlenecks ready for the premiere, because the resulting documentary from A24, “You Can See Everything,” is coming to theaters on October 16.

title: YouTube Music gets more conversational with new AI features
description: YouTube is adding new AI-powered features to YouTube Music that aim to make it easier for listeners to discover music, explore artists, and find podcasts they may otherwise miss. Announced at this year’s Made...
body:
YouTube is adding new AI-powered features to YouTube Music that aim to make it easier for listeners to discover music, explore artists, and find podcasts they may otherwise miss.
Announced at this year’s Made On YouTube event, the updates include “Ask Music,” a conversational tool for music and podcasts, and “Your Podcast Lineup,” a personalized audio guide designed to help listeners discover new shows.
Built directly into the YouTube Music app, Ask Music lets users describe what they want to hear in everyday language rather than searching for individual songs or artists. The feature works across YouTube Music’s catalog of more than 300 million songs, including official recordings, remixes, live performances, covers, and DJ sets. Users can use it to build custom listening queues, explore an artist’s motivations, or dig deeper into music history.
Image Credits:YouTube
YouTube explains that, instead of manually searching, the user simply types the request as if they were asking a friend. For instance, someone could ask Ask Music to create a mix based on the tracks that inspired a particular song. Users can also ask other questions, such as who played bass on a particular song or other details about its creation.
Image Credits:YouTube
YouTube Music is also introducing Your Podcast Lineup, a personalized AI-generated audio guide for podcast discovery.
The feature is designed for a familiar problem: There are more podcasts than most people have time to listen to. Even listeners who already have a list of favorite shows can struggle to keep up with new episodes, let alone find new ones.
Your Podcast Lineup will appear on the podcast page in the YouTube Music app. Each week, it will provide a short spoken preview of recommended shows and explain why they might appeal to the listener. It can then move directly into suggested episodes.
Spotify recently introduced an AI-powered feature that follows a similar direction. Its personal podcasts feature uses AI to generate podcast episodes based on their interests and prompts.
The new features are part of YouTube’s broader push to use AI throughout its services. Last year, YouTube Music experimented with AI-powered music hosts that provide stories, fan trivia, and commentary related to what users are listening to.
Both updates are coming soon to YouTube Music and YouTube Premium subscribers worldwide.

title: YouTube’s conversational video editing tool lets creators make edits in natural language
description: Image Credits:YouTube	 	 						8:46 AM PDT · September 23, 2026											  			 YouTube announced a bunch of new creator tools at Wednesday’s Made On YouTube event, including a conversational editing tool...
body:
Image Credits:YouTube	
	
						8:46 AM PDT · September 23, 2026											

			
YouTube announced a bunch of new creator tools at Wednesday’s Made On YouTube event, including a conversational editing tool that uses natural language to refine both long- and short-form footage.
“A one-hour shoot can be 10 hours or more in the edit. So, what if we could speed that process along without sacrificing any of our creative control?” YouTuber Happy Kelli shared onstage.
In a chat interface, creators give the AI instructions on how to help them put a video together. In Happy Kelli’s example, she shares footage of her dancing in different outfits and asks the AI to select the best take for each outfit. Then, she adds music and transitions that go along with the dance.
Image Credits:YouTube
“If at any point I want even more control, I can jump back into the editing timeline and manually adjust things myself,” she said. “Overall, conversational editing turns the process of editing into a literal conversation with an infinitely patient helper. It’s a collaborative partner that edits with you, not for you.”
This feature can also add text overlays, remove pauses in speech, and more. It can also make suggestions to the creator based on the context of the conversation.
While some creators may find that this tool saves them time and speeds up the often tedious process of video editing, others may feel that their individual editing style sets their videos apart and be reluctant to relinquish control to an AI.
Conversational editing will be available for both YouTube Shorts and the YouTube Create app in early 2027.

title: YouTube adds new creator tools like video A/B testing, dynamic thumbnails, and live dubbing
description: In a bid to help creators reach more people, YouTube on Wednesday unveiled a slew of new tools, many of which use AI to try out different tactics on videos to find what makes them perform best. The new Ask...
body:
In a bid to help creators reach more people, YouTube on Wednesday unveiled a slew of new tools, many of which use AI to try out different tactics on videos to find what makes them perform best. 
The new Ask Studio feature allows creators to share draft videos with AI to get personalized feedback based on their previous content and user comments. The feature will propose alternative titles and thumbnail options, analyze the creator’s channel analytics to explain the performance of their videos, and offer advice for improving metrics. Ask Studio is expanding to YouTube’s mobile apps, too.
Image Credits:YouTube
YouTube already allows creators to A/B test titles and thumbnails, and from 2027, this feature will let creators upload and test three different cuts for Shorts. There’s also a Dynamic Thumbnails feature, with which creators can upload multiple thumbnails and leave it to YouTube to determine which thumbnail to show viewers that is most likely to spark their interest.
Creators can also apply these tools to their existing catalog. If a creator allows it, Ask Studio will be able to autonomously monitor thumbnail performance and create tests to refine older videos.
On the shopping front, YouTube will now use AI to auto-tag products, which it says will help creators earn money through affiliate programs. The company is also expanding its Amazon affiliate program beyond the U.S.
Image Credits:YouTube
Some creators are understandably skeptical of using AI to support their content, worrying that just one AI-generated mistake could harm their credibility. For such features to succeed, they will need to be accurate enough to assuage creators’ concerns.
The platform is also giving creators new ways to go live. Early next year, YouTube will pilot auto-dubbing on live videos to translate creators’ speech into other languages in real time. The company is also launching a “live showdown” feature, which lets creators co-host streams together, and even get paired with other creators currently streaming through “live creator matchmaking.”
“Co-hosts can kick off friendly head-to-head matchups, where viewers send chats, gifts, and Super Chats to push their creator’s score forward on-screen in real time,” YouTube Live product manager Barbara MacDonald wrote in a blog post.
Image Credits:YouTube
Hopefully these impromptu collaborations with strangers won’t turn into a hotbed of bad behavior.
YouTube also shared data that provides insight into how people are using the platform. More people continue to watch YouTube on household TVs, and more than half of the top 100 YouTube creators have “living room” as their most watched interface. 
YouTube’s data also confirms what we know about the growth of the microdrama industry: In the first half of 2026, microdramas on YouTube surpassed 6.5 billion views, and their watch time rose 50% year-over-year. People even seem to be watching these episodic, vertical video series on the big screen, with views of microdrama content on TVs increasing 90% year-over-year.

title: YouTube’s new ‘Shorts series’ feature brings episodic viewing to Shorts
description: As microdrama apps gain traction, YouTube is clearly betting that episodic short-form storytelling will stick around. And that the format belongs on Shorts. At its Made On YouTube event on Wednesday, the...
body:
As microdrama apps gain traction, YouTube is clearly betting that episodic short-form storytelling will stick around. And that the format belongs on Shorts.
At its Made On YouTube event on Wednesday, the company announced “Shorts series,” a new tool that lets creators organize their Shorts into TV-style seasons and episodes. The feature brings a more traditional episodic structure to YouTube Shorts, complete with custom thumbnails and playback.
With Shorts series, viewers can watch a selection of Shorts as a continuous story rather than simply scrolling from one stand-alone clip to the next. The series will live on a creator’s YouTube channel. 
The feature is rolling out to creators in the YouTube Partner Program across web, mobile, and connected TVs.
The move comes as no surprise, given that YouTubers have already been experimenting with microdramas and, increasingly, they’re considering it a serious business venture. 
For instance, internet personality Hannah Stocking has crossed into vertical drama, starring in the musical microdrama “Playback,” which premiered on Holywater’s My Drama platform. Then there’s Joshua Ovenshire (The Jovenshire), a longtime YouTube creator who has moved away from traditional YouTube videos. He now works as an executive producer, making shows for vertical platform ReelShort, including a “Love Island”-inspired series called “Secrets and Soulmates.”
The format has even become popular enough to attract recognizable Hollywood names, with celebrities including James Franco, Issa Rae, and Jesse Tyler Ferguson getting involved.
YouTube’s new feature also puts the platform more directly into competition with a growing collection of microdrama apps. TikTok recently launched PineDrama, its own microdrama app, while others such as ReelShort and DramaBox have also grown in popularity. 
For YouTube, Shorts series could be a way to keep viewers engaged without sending them off to other platforms for episodic vertical storytelling. Instead, they’re providing a way to access it all directly on YouTube. 
The company adds that Shorts series builds on “Creator Shows,” which it announced at its annual upfront event last year. This gave select creators the tools to organize their content into a viewing experience designed for TV. Creators, including Michelle Khare and Rhett & Link, used the tools to structure their content into seasons and episodes, making it easier for viewers to binge on the big screen.
Other Made On YouTube announcements are also designed to help creators grow and engage audiences. This includes “Live Showdowns,” which let creators pair up for interactive team challenges; expanded video A/B testing to compare different cuts or opening hooks; “Dynamic Thumbnails” to allow YouTubers to select the most engaging option from up to three creator-provided thumbnails for different audiences; new shopping features; and more.

title: YouTube releases new AI features for creators within its Studio app
description: Image Credits:YouTube	 	 						7:30 AM PDT · September 23, 2026											  			 At its Made On YouTube annual event, YouTube announced new tools for YouTube Studio, the app creators use to manage their...
body:
Image Credits:YouTube	
	
						7:30 AM PDT · September 23, 2026											

			
At its Made On YouTube annual event, YouTube announced new tools for YouTube Studio, the app creators use to manage their channels, aimed at helping them analyze their videos and grow their audiences. The updates include expanding Ask Studio, its AI-powered Q&A feature, to iOS and Android, as well as new features that provide feedback on drafts and create dynamic thumbnails.
The draft-feedback feature uses AI to look at a creator’s unpublished video and provide suggestions about pacing, structure, and storytelling. YouTube is also debuting a new research feed in the Studio app that shows creators what kind of content is working on the platform, so they can apply their own take on it.
Creators are typically picky about the preview images and titles they use for their videos. The Studio app will now let them generate thumbnails and titles based on a video’s content and matched to their style. Creators can also use a new dynamic thumbnail feature to generate three options and show each one to a different segment of their audience.
Image Credits:YouTube
YouTube said creators have used its A/B testing feature to run more than 40 million tests on titles and thumbnails. Soon, the company said, users will be able to test up to three video cuts to see which opening hook works best. Later this year, YouTube Studio will also automatically monitor thumbnail performance and change one proactively if it doesn’t perform well.
YouTube also said it’s updating its analytics to go beyond raw numbers, explaining why videos perform the way they do and providing advice about how to make content more engaging.
Image Credits:YouTube
Besides the Studio app revamp, YouTube also introduced other tools for creators, including conversational editing in Shorts and the YouTube Create app.

title: Even Americans who use AI every day are worried about it
description: People across the world are increasingly turning to AI for everyday tasks, from looking up recipes and doing their homework to researching work projects or making presentations. But using AI every day...
body:
People across the world are increasingly turning to AI for everyday tasks, from looking up recipes and doing their homework to researching work projects or making presentations. 
But using AI every day doesn’t necessarily mean people are feeling comfortable with its implications for the world: About 68% of Americans who use AI daily are worried about it, according to a new survey conducted by opinion research firm Gallup, and concern about the tech skews even higher among people who use it less frequently. 
Coming at a time of intense debate around the dangers of AI, quick developments around AI safety, the implications of AI going rogue, and accusations of anticompetitive behavior, these findings complicate the notion that adoption can serve as a straightforward measure of public enthusiasm for AI.
Commissioned by Microsoft, the Gallup study currently has results from 37 countries, where researchers polled about 1,000 people in each country between April and July. The project will eventually span 140 countries. Notably, India, a large population of tech users, is not currently part of the reported results, nor are Australia and Malaysia.
The findings appear to put the U.S. at the anxious end of an international chart even as people in other parts of the world expect the technology to improve their lives. According to Gallup, Western countries are most concerned about AI, with the United States leading in anxiety — 74% of Americans reported feelings of worry, and only 36% expect AI to mostly help the country.
Other wealthy Western countries showed a similar mix of relatively frequent use and concern. In Canada, for example, 29% of those surveyed reported using AI daily, and of those, more than half expressed concerns about the impact of the technology. Overall, 64% of Canadians aware of AI said it worried them. 
There’s certainly been a growing wave of discontent around AI, with tech companies laying off hundreds of thousands of employees in order to invest in AI, shrinking entry-level openings, life-ending cases of AI psychosis, and dire warnings from AI leaders like Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, who warned that the tech will wipe out jobs en masse.
The survey paints a different picture in the rest of the world, however. In Singapore, which had the highest portion of daily users in the study (46%), more than 80% of those aware about AI expect the tech to improve their everyday lives, and 77% think it’ll help the country. In China, where 35% of people report using AI daily, most people expect it to help the country. The story is similar in Israel.
Still, optimism about AI doesn’t necessarily appear to translate to trust in the tech’s accuracy. According to Gallup, people who use AI daily were generally more trusting of its results, especially in high-adoption countries like Singapore, Israel, and China, while less frequent users remain skeptical across the board. In the U.S., only 45% of daily users expressed that level of confidence. Altogether, only 36% (median) of the people surveyed said they trust AI’s results a lot.
Overall, though, Gallup reports that positivity about AI outweighs negative sentiments: In 34 of the 37 countries surveyed, people mostly reported feeling curious about the tech, with a fewer number saying they felt happy or excited. Only about 32% of those surveyed said they felt worried about AI. Positive emotions seem to be most common in China (90%), Singapore (89%), and Kenya (87%).
It’s not clear how much sentiment in some countries, especially China, might have changed since the survey ended in July, as the pace of AI development has lately burgeoned into a matter of international importance. AI safety is one of the major topics on the table for discussion when U.S. president Donald Trump and Chinese premier Xi Jinping meet on Thursday.
Notably, China’s head of the Ministry of State Security, Chen Yixin, wrote in a recent article that AI will have “a systemic impact on the political and security environment,” and could threaten China’s “political security, institutional security, and ideological security.”
“One of the clearest findings is that attitudes toward AI are multidimensional. People can be curious about AI, expect it to be beneficial and use it frequently while still being worried about it. Similarly, they can see considerable potential in AI while remaining skeptical about whether the information it provides is accurate,” Pablo Diego-Rosell, senior scientist at Gallup, told TechCrunch. 
While the report paints a picture of optimism colored by some concern, it’s nevertheless true that AI worries are increasingly becoming part of public discourse. People who rely on AI for day-to-day tasks may end up supporting tougher rules or resisting its use in hiring, healthcare, education, or government. And there’s certainly an argument to be made that training and serving AI models can harm the climate, and their unregulated use can disrupt cybersecurity, diminish content ownership, upset the creative arts fields, or harm data privacy.
At the end of the day, the report suggests that greater exposure alone will not resolve the unease around the technology. Still, given the amount of money that’s being invested, AI will likely continue proliferating even as disputes rage around where it belongs and what limits should be placed around it.

title: LinkedIn adds new tools to fight fake profiles and bogus work histories
description: LinkedIn is rolling out new verification tools that let members vouch for colleagues’ work experience and give companies more control over accounts that falsely claim to employ them.
body:
AI has made it significantly easier for people to create fake accounts and identities to engage in online manipulation and scams. On Wednesday, LinkedIn announced a new set of tools to combat the problem while helping people and companies better control their presence on the platform.
The company says it will now let members vouch for each other’s experience and give businesses new controls to manage who associates with their brand, among other changes.
The new features arrive at a time when impersonation has become an internet-wide problem, not one limited to LinkedIn. However, on a network where your professional persona includes your work experience, past job titles, certifications, university degrees, and more, being able to verify you are who you say you are is even more critical. 
Such claims can lead to career opportunities and advancement, prospects that those fudging or lying on their resumes haven’t earned.
“The backdrop for all this is that faking credibility has never been cheaper or easier than it is today; and conversely, showcasing credibility has never mattered more,” LinkedIn VP of Product Oscar Rodriguez told TechCrunch in an interview.
To date, LinkedIn’s existing verification tools have been used to verify 115 million users and over 700,000 companies on the platform, he noted. 
“We’ve been invested in [verification] because we believe that authenticity will be the single most valuable currency on the internet,” Rodriguez added.
Image Credits:LinkedIn
For starters, LinkedIn will now allow members to vouch for their colleagues and classmates, past or present. This feature is not the same as an endorsement, where you can recommend the member to others, but is more of a way to vouch that someone has the experience they claim on their profile. 
In short, it’s a way of saying, “Yes, I worked with this person during this time,” not whether you enjoyed it. 
The addition includes a number of built-in protections against abuse. For instance, the person doing the vouching must already have a verified profile, and they must have been connected to the person for at least a year. They also have to have a secure account that uses two-factor authentication to decrease the risk of hackers gaining access to their account to perform these vouches. 
Image Credits:LinkedIn
Another feature, which had previously been piloted with recruiters and execs, will allow companies to remove accounts that falsely claim employment from appearing on their page and in the search results associated with their page. 
To use this feature, page admins will be able to visit the account that belongs to the person falsely claiming employment at the company, then manually remove them. LinkedIn is also testing a setting that will allow page admins to require that any member account going forward that tries to associate with the page complete some sort of workplace verification, like a verification done through their work email address. 
When pages remove the member profile from their page, it won’t change the member’s LinkedIn profile — that’s something members themselves will retain control over. However, there will no longer be a clickable link to that company’s page from their profile, and their work experience won’t display as verified. 
Image Credits:LinkedIn
“We hope that this provides signals and context to members to make decisions,” Rodriguez said. He also clarified this feature focuses on full-time employees, not contractors or field workers, though they will have other means of claiming their rightful association with the company that employs them.  
Plus, LinkedIn will expand its partnerships with more companies to allow members to showcase their verified identities beyond LinkedIn. On this front, Truecaller and PeerSpot will join existing partners like Adobe and UserTesting in this effort. For instance, Truecaller members can add their LinkedIn verified identity so it displays to the recipient when they place a call. 
Overall, the new features expand LinkedIn’s push to invest in verification, something that it believes benefits members directly. “We have seen how, for members that are verified, they derive a lot of benefits from all of this,” said Rodriguez. “They receive, on average, 50% more post views than non-verified profiles, and they get 90% more impressions as well,” he noted.

title: Eight Sleep’s new Pod 6 comes in smaller and solo sizes, starting at $1,999
description: Sleep tech company Eight Sleep on Wednesday launched its new Pod 6 device in a smaller size than previous editions to fit more bed frames, along with solo sizes for one-person use. The company said that the...
body:
Sleep tech company Eight Sleep on Wednesday launched its new Pod 6 device in a smaller size than previous editions to fit more bed frames, along with solo sizes for one-person use. The company said that the device can be used to adjust the temperature on either side 20% faster than the previous-generation gadget.
Because the new pod has a 50% smaller footprint, it can fit most bed frames. The company claims the device has 9x more sensors, enabling it to understand granular temperature controls for each user even if they are sleeping close together. Plus, it can ignore data from a pet or a kid sleeping on the bed with two users.
The Pod 6 is available starting today in over 37 countries, starting at $1,999 for solo sizes and $2,699 for standard sizes. Solo sizes can fit a twin bed and one side of queen, king, and California King beds. Standard sizes will be available in queen, king, and California King. Plus, it can work with existing add-ons like a blanket, pillow cover, and base.
Image Credits:Eight Sleep
Beyond new sleep products, the company is pursuing Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approval to transition its Eight Sleep Pod into a regulated medical device for sleep apnea in the U.S. 
Earlier this year, the company raised $50 million from Tether at a $1.5 billion valuation. Eight Sleep also took steps to expand its international footprint by launching its product in China, Qatar, Bahrain, Kuwait, and Singapore in the last year, with China becoming one of the fastest-growing regions.
The company’s CEO Matteo Franceschetti told TechCrunch that international markets contribute over 30% of revenue. He mentioned that the sleep tech company plans to expand into other regions of Asia and Latin America. Franceschetti noted that the company is keeping a keen eye on the component crunch in the electronics sector, but didn’t say whether it will impact pricing. 
“We definitely see the market changing a little bit because AI companies are requesting a lot of different components. We are adjusting our supply chain [to counter that]. It’s definitely something that we need to watch out for, particularly as our devices become more and more, I would say, compute-heavy and intelligent to be able to provide AI features to our users,” he said.

title: YouTube doubles down on video shopping with AI-powered ‘Ask YouTube’ feature
description: “Ask YouTube,” the video site’s newer AI-powered conversational search feature, will become a shopping companion, the company announced on Wednesday at its Made On YouTube event. Ask YouTube began as an...
body:
“Ask YouTube,” the video site’s newer AI-powered conversational search feature, will become a shopping companion, the company announced on Wednesday at its Made On YouTube event.
Ask YouTube began as an experiment in conversational search, before becoming a larger part of the YouTube experience. The feature allows anyone to search YouTube using natural language requests, including with queries that are more complex and detailed than in traditional search. YouTube will then compile a set of results that may include both Shorts and long-form videos, guiding you through topics like step-by-step travel plans, guides to learning a new skill, or a series of recommendations around particular topics.
Now, the company says Ask YouTube will gain more features that will help users as they make shopping decisions. For instance, if you search for a particular product, you might receive organized recommendations that include things like a comparison table showing various product attributes or categories, based on your preferences.
You’ll also be able to ask follow-up questions directly on that video’s watch page. 
YouTube says the changes are based on trends it’s already seeing in user behavior, as they learn from creators about different products, trusting their opinions and recommendations. Already, over 140 million people have used Ask YouTube to dive in deeper to videos during the month of June, the company noted — a jump of more than 500% since last December.
“Behind that growth is a custom Gemini model that maps the viewer’s most complex questions to the exact second that the video provides the answer, turning a passive search into an instant, meaningful connection with the video and with the creator,” explained Emily Moxley, VP of Product Management for Viewer AI at YouTube, in a briefing with reporters ahead of today’s event.

title: Modal Motors is trying to cut China out of electric motors entirely
description: Lately, it seems like everyone is talking about bringing manufacturing back to the United States, especially when it comes to hard tech like drones and robotics. Michael Van Steenburg thinks he’s ahead of the...
body:
Lately, it seems like everyone is talking about bringing manufacturing back to the United States, especially when it comes to hard tech like drones and robotics. Michael Van Steenburg thinks he’s ahead of the game. 
Van Steenburg spent the last decade building all kinds of electric motors in the U.S. and North America, and now he wants to do it again with his new startup, Modal Motors. This time, he wants to ditch rare earth magnets entirely, in a bid to further separate the U.S. from China’s supply chain.
As one of founders in Startup Battlefield 200 who will compete at TechCrunch Disrupt next month, he thinks it’s an urgent pitch to make.
“China’s already flexed its muscles a couple times,” Van Steenburg said, referring to the country restricting access to rare earth products.
There are other companies working on setting up electric motor manufacturing and supply chains in the U.S., but Van Steenburg argues they’re doing it the wrong way by continuing to rely on rare earth magnets. Domestic supply of those materials is still years away, he said.
“Other people are ‘reshoring,’ [but] they’re basically knocking off Chinese motors and just doing it in the U.S. But they’re hoping that the U.S. rare earth magnet system is going to get up to speed fast enough,” he said. “It’s going to still be a while longer before they can actually replace China.”
Modal Motors has two products that it’s developing ahead of Disrupt. One is a small electric motor meant for drones that can also work in fans, blowers, and even actuators. It’s designed to “minimize mass while delivering maximum torque density and efficiency,” according to the startup’s website.
The more radical design is what Modal refers to as the “Hybrid Enigma Drive,” a planar — or flat — electric motor that can fit in lower-profile spaces.
Van Steenburg is drawing on decades of experience in the automotive industry to develop these motors and get them customer-ready. But there’s also an irony in the work Van Steenburg is doing to make Modal Motors’ products a China-free option; in the late 1990s, he worked on a hybrid gas-electric drivetrain that China wanted to put in its so-called “People’s Car.”
“It’s kind of comical,” he said, thinking back on that experience and how much the world has changed. What hasn’t changed, he said, is his outsider streak and strong conviction about doing things that are hard.
“I always tell people that the clock started ticking 25 years ago, and in that whole time, I’ve watched a slow-motion train wreck as China’s been going around the world, grabbing mines, grabbing mineral rights, doing all these things, and slowly but surely monopolizing the entire rare earth supply chain,” he said.
